analysis.title: AI and productivity: Productivity growth remains concentrated in high-AI exposed industries
key_insights: Output per employee is rising faster in industries Morgan Stanley classes as high-AI exposure than in mid- or low-AI industries. The acceleration was larger in 2025 and remains stronger.
Economy-wide output/employee rose 2.4% y/y through 2Q 2026. That matches the pace of 2Q 2025, is below the 3.0% y/y of 1Q 2026, and is about twice the average pace of the past twenty years.

High-AI industries contributed 2.0pp of the 2.4% rise in output per employee over the past four quarters. Mid- and low-AI industries together contributed 0.4pp. A year earlier the split was 1.4pp for high-AI and 1.0pp for mid and low combined.

With two more quarters of data and the GDP annual revision, the contribution of high-AI industries to overall productivity is larger and the acceleration in their output is bigger than in the bank's first update six months ago.

The productivity pickup reflects faster output growth and capital deepening, but there is now some labor displacement in high-AI industries. Employment in these industries is declining and contributing more to productivity growth than before.

About half of the industries classed as high AI-exposed are seeing employment declines, with no clear common theme. The bank calls the labor replacement 'micro' rather than macro, but a more evident threat than six months ago.

Labor replacement looks likely in data processing and software (jobs falling at an increasing rate amid rapid output gains) and in credit intermediation (commercial banking and mortgage employment weak, though this may reflect a weak housing market).
Employment weakness in private education (federal oversight, shrinking youth population) and management (stalled after prior gains) is less likely to be attributable to AI.

Computer manufacturing is accelerating hiring tied to the AI infrastructure buildout, but its output and productivity both fell. Securities has rising output and payrolls. Legal services has stalled output but rising payrolls.

The annual GDP revision lifted output per employee from late 2023 on. Earlier estimates showed 0.3-0.5pp slower growth in output and output per employee in 2023-24. The upward revisions were in mid-AI industries, not high-AI, and the 2023 pickup seems too early to reflect AI. The bank suspects it reflected pandemic-era efficiency and cost control.

Real GDP grew 2.1% over the past four quarters, close to the bank's estimate of potential growth. The bank reads the strength as a supply-side impulse from faster productivity, not overheating demand.

The labor market has been strong enough to absorb employment strains from AI-exposed industries and age groups: the unemployment rate has fallen slightly over the past year and the payrolls pace has picked up a bit.

Method: output per employee uses BEA industry output and BLS payrolls across 64 industries (12 high, 26 low, 26 medium AI exposure), with exposure scores from Felten et al. (2021). Output per employee is an imperfect proxy for output per hour.

sector_views.rationale: They account for 2.0pp of the 2.4% productivity gain, driven mostly by faster output and capital deepening in AI-related industries.
Their contributions to productivity are diminishing. Mid-AI shows stalled employment growth and slowing output growth, and low-AI shows weak output and stalled employment.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Equal to the 2Q 2025 pace, below 3.0% in 1Q 2026, and twice the 20-year average. Points to a supply-side productivity impulse.
The recent peak of the proxy measure, above the 2Q reading.
Close to the bank's estimate of potential growth, so the growth is not from overheating demand.
Down from 2.8% in 1Q 2026 and 2.4% in 4Q 2025. The bank's proxy has a strong enough link to it to draw industry-level inferences.
Versus 7.8% in 1Q 2026 and 7.0% in 4Q 2025, so still very strong but off the 1Q peak.

risk_factors: Labor replacement in high-AI industries is a more evident threat than six months ago, including upward pressure on unemployment for young workers in high-AI-exposure occupations.
Output per employee is an imperfect proxy for output per hour, the preferred productivity measure.
Industry-level data are subject to revisions, as the annual GDP revision showed.
Some employment declines in high-AI industries (credit intermediation, private education) may reflect non-AI causes such as a weak housing market or funding threats.

tension_points.bull_case: Productivity gains come mainly from faster output and capital deepening in high-AI industries. High-AI industries supplied 2.0pp of the 2.4% rise, and the labor market has absorbed the strain.
tension_points.bear_case: Employment is now falling in about half of high-AI industries, notably data processing, software and credit intermediation, and young workers in AI-exposed occupations face upward pressure on unemployment.

theme_stances.key_argument: Productivity growth is concentrated in high-AI exposed industries and comes mainly from faster output, with labor displacement a distant secondary factor.
theme_stances.evidence: The predominant story to strong productivity growth in high-AI industries is faster output growth.

theme_stances.key_argument: Some labor replacement is now visible in high-AI industries, though the bank calls it a micro effect, not a macro one.
theme_stances.evidence: Labor displacement is playing a distant secondary role.
